query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A minor addition of a ductile, high thermal conductivity element (e.g., 2–5 atomic % Cu) to the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high‐entropy alloy will enable the in‐situ formation of a two‐phase composite microstructure that reinforces grain boundaries and arrests crack propagation, thereby significantly improving its structural integrity without appreciably reducing its large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy that produces a strong caloric effect under applied-field and pressure-field operation but suffers from poor mechanical integrity (low compressive strength and crack susceptibility).
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled 2–5 at.% Cu during alloy processing so that upon solidification Cu segregates and forms an interconnected ductile phase.
generation.conditions: Tests performed under the same applied magnetic and pressure fields and typical thermal cycling conditions where the original caloric response is measured; mechanical loading conditions similar to previous compressive tests (ambient to moderately elevated temperatures).
generation.structural_mediator: An in-situ, finely dispersed Cu-rich ductile phase distributed along grain boundaries and/or as an interpenetrating network within the primary high-entropy matrix.
generation.mechanism: The Cu addition is expected to segregate during processing to form a continuous ductile network that enhances crack arrest and improves compressive strength by bridging grain boundaries. This microstructural modification should preserve the phase transformation or lattice responses governing the caloric effect, thus maintaining its large caloric performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is predicted to show a significant increase in compressive strength (targeting values above 220 MPa) and enhanced fracture toughness, while the magnitude of the caloric response is reduced by less than ~10% compared to the base alloy.
generation.baseline: The unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits a large caloric response but, as previously observed in related systems (e.g., epoxy-containing composites achieving 152–218 MPa), suffers from limited mechanical integrity and crack sensitivity.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected to hold under typical field-induced caloric operating conditions and standard mechanical loading; however, performance may diverge if the Cu content exceeds ~5 at.% or under conditions where extensive segregation alters the primary transformation underlying the caloric effect.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty about the exact optimum Cu content and the kinetics of phase segregation during processing. It is possible that interactions between Cu and the base elements could locally modify the microstructure in unforeseen ways that might affect the caloric effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples using identical processing conditions: one set with 2–5 at.% Cu added to the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy and a control set without Cu. Conduct compressive mechanical tests and caloric response measurements (under the same applied magnetic and pressure-field conditions) on both sets.
measurements: Compressive yield strength and plasticity (e.g., via compression tests)
Crack initiation and propagation behavior (via microscopy, e.g., SEM/TEM)
Caloric response metrics (temperature change, entropy change under field cycling)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cu-added samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in mechanical integrity (e.g., compressive strength improvement >10–20% relative to the control) or if the caloric response is degraded by more than 10% compared to the unmodified alloy, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

The microstructure, Vickers hardness, and compressive properties of novel low-activation VCrFeTaxWx (x = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, and 1) high-entropy alloys (HEAs) were studied. The alloys were fabricated by vacuum-arc melting and the characteristics of these alloys were explored. The microstructures of all the alloys exhibited a typical morphology of dendritic and eutectic structures. The VCrFeTa0.1W0.1 and VCrFeTa0.2W0.2 alloys are essentially single phase, consisting of a disordered body-centered-cubic (BCC) phase, whereas the VCrFeTa0.2W0.2 alloy contains fine, nanoscale precipitates distributed in the BCC matrix. The lattice parameters and compositions of the identified phases were investigated. The alloys have Vickers hardness values ranging from 546 HV0.2 to 1135 HV0.2 with the x ranging from 0.1 to 1, respectively. The VCrFeTa0.1W0.1 and VCrFeTa0.2W0.2 alloys exhibit compressive yield strengths of 1341 MPa and 1742 MPa, with compressive plastic strains of 42.2% and 35.7%, respectively.
